summary: Croatia lies in the north-west of the Balkan Peninsula on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, has a long coastline and historic old towns such as Dubrovnik, and became independent from Yugoslavia in 1991.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The Croats accepted Christianity in the 7th–9th centuries, and in 879 Pope John VIII recognized the rule of Duke Branimir, after which Croatia was closely tied to the Holy See and long preserved the Slavic liturgy using the Glagolitic script. From the 16th century Croatia stood on the front line against the Ottoman Empire, and in 1519 it was called the "bulwark of Christendom" by the Pope. The church was suppressed in the communist Yugoslav period, and in the war of independence in the 1990s Catholicism became a marker of national identity distinguishing Croats from Serbian Orthodoxy, so the proportion is very high.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: From 1945 to 1991 the communist Yugoslav regime pursued a policy of secularization, and some families therefore lost their religious heritage. The non-religious are concentrated in the capital Zagreb and more open urban areas such as Istria and Rijeka, mainly among the young and highly educated.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Orthodox believers are mainly ethnic Serbs. From the 16th century the Habsburgs settled large numbers of Serb and Vlach border-guard colonists in the "Military Frontier" against the Ottomans, which rooted Orthodoxy in Croatian territory. In 1991 Serbs made up a little over a tenth of the population, but after "Operation Storm" in 1995 about two hundred thousand Serbs left, and the proportion of Orthodox fell sharply.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Austria-Hungary formally recognized Islam as a legal religion in 1916. The Muslims are mostly Bosniaks and Albanians who migrated from Bosnia, Kosovo and elsewhere in the 20th century, and the Zagreb mosque, completed in 1987, is the center of the local Islamic community.

religion.background: Croatia lies at the boundary between Catholic Western Europe and the Orthodox and Islamic worlds. In the Middle Ages the Kingdom of Croatia accepted Roman Catholicism, after the union with Hungary in 1102 it long belonged to the Catholic Habsburg world, and the Ottoman invasions made religion a symbol of resistance against the foreign enemy. The establishment of the Military Frontier brought Orthodox Serbs. In the Yugoslav period of the 20th century the communist regime suppressed religion, and after independence in 1991 the status of the Catholic Church rose greatly, and the population changes caused by the war also made Croatia a country with a very high proportion of Catholics.

ranking.name: Croatian
ranking.description: Croatian belongs to the South Slavic branch; the Baška tablet of around 1100, carved in the Glagolitic script, is the most important early document, and Marulić's epic Judita of 1501 is regarded as the work of the father of Croatian literature. The "Illyrian movement" led by Ljudevit Gaj in the 1830s established a writing system in the Latin alphabet with diacritics. In the Yugoslav period it was called "Serbo-Croatian" together with Serbian, in 1967 intellectuals issued a declaration demanding recognition of its independent status, and after independence in 1991 it became the sole official language.

ranking.name: Serbian
ranking.description: Serbian is highly mutually intelligible with Croatian and is used mainly by the Serb minority, traditionally written in the Cyrillic script. After the mass departure of Serbs in 1995 the number of users fell greatly; the protests when Cyrillic bilingual signs were installed in Vukovar in 2013 showed the linguistic sensitivity under the memory of the war.

language.history: The Slavs migrated into the Balkans in the 7th century, and the early Croats wrote in the Glagolitic script, forming a distinctive liturgical and literary tradition. Croatian has three major dialects, Štokavian, Kajkavian and Čakavian; in the Middle Ages and Renaissance the literature of the Dalmatian coast was influenced by Venice, while the interior was influenced by Hungarian and German. In the 19th century the national revival movement established a standard language based on the Štokavian dialect. In the Yugoslav period of the 20th century it was merged with Serbian into one standard language, and after independence in 1991 Croatian again became an independent national language.

ranking.name: Pašticada (braised beef)
ranking.description: Beef is marinated in vinegar overnight, stuffed with garlic, cloves and bacon, and then slowly stewed for hours with red wine, dried plums and root vegetables, and served with potato gnocchi.
ranking.history: Pašticada is a representative dish of Dalmatia, especially Split, and its preparation often takes two days. The Dalmatian coast was long ruled by the Republic of Venice (15th–18th centuries), and the spices and wine-braising method used in this dish reflect Venetian and Mediterranean influence. It is traditionally a feast dish prepared for weddings, festivals and important family gatherings, and every family has its own secret recipe.

ranking.name: Štrukli
ranking.description: Thin dough wrapped around fresh farmhouse cheese, egg and sour cream, rolled up and cut into pieces and boiled, or topped with cream and baked, with a rich, soft texture.
ranking.history: Štrukli originated in the Zagorje region north of Zagreb and around the capital, and is a traditional farmhouse dish of northern Croatia. From the 19th century it went from a country food to a dish loved by the urban middle class of Zagreb, and today it has been listed as Croatian intangible cultural heritage and is protected. It is a representative dish of Zagreb restaurants and Sunday family lunches.

ranking.name: Fritule (fried dough balls)
ranking.description: A batter with raisins, lemon zest and rum is spooned into hot oil and fried into small balls, then dusted with powdered sugar, crisp outside and soft inside, sweet and delicious.
ranking.history: Fritule originated on the Dalmatian and Istrian coasts and shares its origin with Venetian "frittelle", reflecting centuries of Venetian cultural influence on the eastern Adriatic coast. They are traditionally made in Advent before Christmas and on Christmas Eve, and are also a seasonal treat during carnival. Today fritule are one of the most popular snacks at Christmas markets.

ranking.name: Sarma (cabbage rolls)
ranking.description: Whole pickled sour cabbage leaves are rolled around minced pork and beef with rice, and slowly stewed for hours with smoked meat and paprika; the flavor is tangy and rich.
ranking.history: Sarma originates in the Ottoman "dolma" (stuffed dishes), came to the Balkans with Ottoman power, and the name also comes from the Turkish word meaning "to roll". Croats combined it with the winter tradition of pickling whole heads of sour cabbage, making it a representative winter dish. It always appears at Christmas, New Year and winter family gatherings, often stewed in a big pot at a time, and the hotter it is the better it tastes.

ranking.name: Ćevapčići
ranking.description: Small sausage-shaped rolls of minced beef or lamb, charcoal-grilled and served in flatbread with onion and red pepper relish (ajvar).
ranking.history: Ćevapčići originated from the Ottoman kebab, and the name also comes from Turkish; it developed into its present form in Bosnia. In the Yugoslav period, migrants from Bosnia brought it to all parts of Croatia, and it became one of the most popular street grills. Today it is a common food for Croats at summer barbecues and beach holidays, showing the food culture shared across the former Yugoslav region.
